lead: Flow control stops the sender from overwhelming the receiver. It limits how many frames can be in transit before an acknowledgement is required. Stop‑and‑wait uses a single outstanding frame. Sliding‑window lets several frames be sent before waiting. These mechanisms keep the link efficient and avoid buffer overflow in routers, switches, or end‑devices such as a mobile phone receiving video over 4G.
prereq: You need: Framing and bit stuffing and Error detection.

blocks.text: The sender transmits one data frame and then stops. It waits for an acknowledgement (ACK) from the receiver before sending the next frame. The sender starts a timer after sending. If the timer expires before the ACK arrives, the sender retransmits the same frame.

items: Receiver sends cumulative ACK with the next expected sequence number.
Timeout = round‑trip time (RTT) plus a safety margin.

blocks.where: η is link efficiency; a = propagation delay ÷ transmission time; the factor 2 accounts for forward and return propagation.

items: Sender puts frame in the channel.
If correct, receiver sends ACK with seq = next frame number.
Sender receives ACK and proceeds; otherwise timer triggers retransmission.

blocks.text: Stop‑and‑wait is simple but inefficient when the propagation delay is large compared to the transmission time. It is used in low‑speed links such as satellite control channels or simple UART communication.

The sender may transmit up to N frames before waiting for an ACK. N is the sender window size. Each frame carries a sequence number. The receiver acknowledges the highest in‑order sequence received (cumulative ACK).

items: Sender window slides forward when ACKs arrive.
Receiver expects frames in order; out‑of‑order frames are discarded.
If a frame is lost, the receiver discards it and all later frames until the missing one is received.

blocks.where: η is efficiency; N is window size; a is as defined for stop‑and‑wait.

items: Receiver sends ACK = k where k is the next expected sequence number.

When ACK = k arrives, the sender slides its window so that the lowest unacknowledged sequence number becomes k. It can then transmit any new frames with sequence numbers from k up to k+N‑1 that have not been sent yet.

blocks.text: Sliding‑window improves utilization on long‑delay links such as fiber‑optic backbones or Wi‑Fi video streaming. It is the basis for protocols like TCP and HDLC.

examples.question: A link runs at 1 Mbps. Each frame carries 1000 bits of payload. The one‑way propagation delay is 20 ms. Compute the transmission time, the ratio a, and the stop‑and‑wait efficiency η (in %).
steps: Transmission time = frame size ÷ link rate = 1000 bits ÷ 1 Mbps = 0.001 s = 1 ms.
a = propagation delay ÷ transmission time = 20 ms ÷ 1 ms = 20.

traps: Using only the forward propagation delay when calculating a makes a too small, which inflates the estimated efficiency.
Confusing the sequence number in the ACK with the number of frames sent; the ACK carries the next expected sequence number.
Assuming the window size N can be larger than the sequence number space without wrap‑around handling.
Treating the timeout as only the propagation delay; it must include transmission time of the frame and processing delays.

quiz.q: What is the size of the sender window in stop‑and‑wait flow control?
quiz.a: The sender window size is 1 frame.

quiz.q: Explain why the efficiency of stop‑and‑wait decreases when the propagation delay grows.
quiz.a: Longer propagation delay means the sender spends more time waiting for ACK while the link is idle, so the fraction of time used for useful data (efficiency) drops.

quiz.q: A 10 Mbps link carries 5000‑bit frames. The one‑way delay is 5 ms. Compute the stop‑and‑wait efficiency.
If the sliding‑window size is 5 and a = 3, what is the approximate efficiency?
Compare stop‑and‑wait and sliding‑window when the link delay‑to‑transmission ratio a = 0.5. Which gives higher throughput and why?
quiz.a: Stop‑and‑wait η = 1 ÷ (1+2×0.5) = 1/2 = 50 %. Sliding‑window with N = 4 (typical minimum) η ≈ 4 ÷ (4+1) = 4/5 = 80 %. Sliding‑window is higher because multiple frames keep the link busy while ACKs travel.

quiz.q: What does a cumulative ACK indicate in sliding‑window protocols?
quiz.a: It acknowledges all frames up to, but not including, the sequence number in the ACK; the receiver expects that number next.

quiz.q: Name one protocol that uses sliding‑window flow control at the data link layer.
quiz.a: HDLC (High‑Level Data Link Control) uses sliding‑window flow control.

beyond: Not for the exam. In modern networks, sliding‑window flow control is combined with congestion control to avoid overload of intermediate routers. Research explores adaptive window sizing based on real‑time RTT measurements for 5G and IoT links. Software‑defined networking can adjust window parameters on the fly to meet service‑level agreements. Look for papers on "dynamic flow control" and the latest revisions of IEEE 802.1Qbb (Priority Flow Control).
